newsitem.title: UK: Environment may change genes, researchers say.
newsitem.headline: Environment may change genes, researchers say.

text.p: British researchers said on Thursday they had found astonishing evidence that environment can affect genes.
They said their findings could explain some things that have long mystified doctors -- such as why the grandchildren of women who starved during World War One are smaller than average.
"This extremely important finding shows that genes are not enough," Lawrence Hurst, a geneticist at the University of Bath, told New Scientist magazine.
Wolf Reik of the Babraham Institute near Cambridge, along with colleagues at the Free University of Berlin, were studying cloned mice.
The clones were produced using established technology that involves removing the nucleus from the cell of an embryo and transplanting it into the cell of another mouse embryo.
Animals produced using this method tend to be abnormal -- they are larger or smaller than usual.
The method used to produce Dolly the cloned sheep, whose birth created a global uproar last month, involves adult cells and is also only partly successful.

Scientists reckoned that something about the environment of the cell itself must be affecting the development of the clones. Reik's group said they had tracked down two genes that are affected by the environment of the nucleus.
They are the gene for a liver protein known as MUP and another called olfactory marker protein (OMP). Both were turned off in the cloned embryos, they reported.
"It took us a long time to believe it," Reik told New Scientist. "The mechanism is wide open."

But he said it could explain influences passed down through generations. One such influence, well-documented, is that pregnant women who starved in Holland during German occupation in World War One produced smaller babies.
That was not surprising, but their grandchildren were also unusually small.
